summary.text: For any divisor-sum representation, either its divisors already have least common multiple equal to the sum, or their least common multiple is a proper divisor and hence at most half the sum; thus it suffices to build an LCM-valid representation at most twice the least integer \(H\) having at least \(n\) divisors. Minimality forces \(H\) to have consecutive prime support with decreasing, explicitly bounded exponents; complete subset-sum divisor sets, disjoint equal-sum padding triples, and an inverse-square-root moment estimate give the construction for at least 25 prime factors, while finite enumeration and divisor-subset searches handle the shorter and exceptional cases and isolate \(n=4,5\) as the only strict ones.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\tau(m)\) denote the number of positive divisors of \(m\). Call a pair \((m,D)\) an ordinary \(n\)-representation if \(m>0\), \(D\) is a set of \(n\) distinct positive divisors of \(m\), and
\[
 \sum_{d\in D}d=m.
\]
Call it a primitive \(n\)-representation if, in addition,
\[
 \operatorname {lcm}_{d\in D}d=m.
\]
Thus \(\mathrm{A081512}(n)\) is the least \(m\) admitting an ordinary \(n\)-representation (or \(0\) if none exists), while \(a(n)\) is the corresponding least \(m\) admitting a primitive representation.

We prove
\[
 a(n)>\mathrm{A081512}(n)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\in\{4,5\}.
\]
The main part of the proof is a uniform domination result: except for \(n=4,5\), every ordinary \(n\)-representation can be replaced by a primitive one at no larger an integer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Reduction to the least integer with \(n\) divisors
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(n\ge0\), let \(H_n\) be the least positive integer satisfying \(\tau(H_n)\ge n\), whenever such an integer is needed. More generally, say that \(H\) is \(n\)-minimal if
\[
 H>0,\qquad \tau(H)\ge n,
\]
and every positive \(K\) with \(\tau(K)\ge n\) satisfies \(H\le K\).

We shall prove the following key assertion.

**Twice-bound theorem.** If \(n\ge3\) and
\[
 n\notin E:=\{4,5,8,9,10,16,20,24,30\},
\]
then for every \(n\)-minimal \(H\), the integer \(2H\) has a primitive \(n\)-representation.

First let us explain why this gives the desired domination. Suppose \(D\) is an ordinary \(n\)-representation at \(m\), and put
\[
 k=\operatorname {lcm}_{d\in D}d.
\]
Every member of \(D\) divides \(k\), and \(k\mid m\). If \(k=m\), the representation is already primitive. Otherwise, since \(k\) is a proper positive divisor of \(m\),
\[
 2k\le m.
\]
Also \(D\) consists of \(n\) distinct divisors of \(k\), so \(\tau(k)\ge n\). Choose an \(n\)-minimal \(H\le k\). By the twice-bound theorem there is a primitive \(n\)-representation at \(2H\), and
\[
 2H\le2k\le m.
\]
Thus every ordinary representation is dominated by a primitive one.

The exceptional values \(8,9,10,16,20,24,30\) will be handled directly. The cases \(n=0,1,2\) are elementary. For \(n=0\), no positive integer can be the sum of an empty set, so there is no ordinary representation. For \(n=1\), an ordinary representation is \(D=\{m\}\), whose lcm is already \(m\). For \(n=2\), no ordinary representation exists: if \(x,y\) are distinct positive divisors of \(m=x+y\), then both are proper divisors, hence \(2x\le m\) and \(2y\le m\); adding gives equality throughout, so \(x=y=m/2\), a contradiction.

It remains to prove the twice-bound theorem and then treat the finite exceptional cases.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Structure of an \(n\)-minimal integer
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write the primes in increasing order as
\[
 p_0=2,p_1=3,p_2=5,p_3=7,\ldots.
\]
If \(H\) is \(n\)-minimal, its prime divisors form an initial segment
\[
 p_0,p_1,\ldots,p_{r-1},
\]
and
\[
 H=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}p_i^{e_i}
\]
with
\[
 e_0\ge e_1\ge\cdots\ge e_{r-1}\ge1.
\]
Indeed, if primes \(p<q\) occur with the exponent of \(q\) larger than that of \(p\), interchanging the two exponents preserves \(\tau(H)=\prod(e_i+1)\) and strictly decreases the integer. In particular, if a prime \(q\) occurs while a smaller prime \(p\) does not, replacing \(q\) by \(p\) decreases the integer without changing its divisor count. Both conclusions contradict minimality.

Two further replacement arguments give useful exponent bounds. If a prime \(q\mid H\), then for every prime \(p\),
\[
 q\le p^{v_p(H)+1}.                                      \tag{1}
\]
For otherwise, if \(a=v_p(H)\) and \(b=v_q(H)>0\), replacing the factor \(q^b\) by \(p^{b(a+1)}\) preserves the relevant divisor-count product, since
\[
 (a+b(a+1)+1)\ge(a+1)(b+1),
\]
but decreases the integer because \(p^{a+1}<q\).

Conversely, suppose \(q\nmid H\), \(p\ne q\), and \(q<p^s\), where \(s>0\). Replacing \(p^a\), where \(a=v_p(H)\), by \(p^{a-s}q\) shows that
\[
 a+2\le2s.                                                \tag{2}
\]
If this failed, then \(a+1\le2(a-s+1)\), so the divisor count would not decrease, while \(q<p^s\) would make the new integer smaller.

Taking \(q=p_{r-1}\) in (1) and the absent prime \(p_r\) in (2) yields, for \(i<r\),
\[
 \log_{p_i}p_{r-1}\le e_i\le2\log_{p_i}p_r,              \tag{3}
\]
where the logarithms are integral floors. These bounds, together with the monotonicity of the \(e_i\), make the set of possible exponent vectors finite for each fixed \(r\).

We also need
\[
 \tau(H)<2n\qquad(H>1).                                  \tag{4}
\]
Let \(a=v_2(H)>0\), and remove one factor 2, obtaining \(K=H/2<H\). By minimality, \(\tau(K)<n\). Since
\[
 \tau(H)=(a+1)\tau(H/2^a),\qquad
 \tau(K)=a\tau(H/2^a),
\]
and \(a+1\le2a\), (4) follows.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Complete coin sets and padding triples
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A finite set \(S\) of positive integers is called complete if every integer from \(0\) through \(\sum S\) is the sum of a subset of \(S\). Starting with the empty set, completeness is preserved when a new element \(x\) is inserted provided
\[
 x\le1+\sum S.                                            \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, sums not exceeding \(\sum S\) are already available, and a larger target \(t\) is obtained by adjoining \(x\) to a subset summing to \(t-x\).

For
\[
 H=\prod_{i<r}p_i^{e_i},
\]
define the coin cost
\[
 C(H)=e_0+1+\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}e_i\bigl(\lfloor\log_2p_i\rfloor+1\bigr). \tag{6}
\]
There is a complete set \(A\) of divisors of \(H\), of cardinality at most \(C(H)\), such that every member of \(A\) is at most \(H\) and
\[
 \sum A+1\ge2H.                                          \tag{7}
\]
Here is the construction. For a power \(2^a\), use the binary coins
\(1,2,4,\ldots,2^a\). If a current complete divisor set reaches a number \(M=2^aC\), and a new odd prime \(p<2^{a+1}\) is introduced, put \(b=\lfloor\log_2p\rfloor\). The divisor
\[
 z=pC2^{a-b}
\]
lies strictly between \(M\) and \(2M\). Adjoin \(z\), and then \(2z,4z,\ldots,2^bz\). Repeated use of (5) extends completeness up to \(Mp\), at a cost of \(b+1\) coins. Repeating this \(e_i\) times for each odd prime power gives (6) and (7). Inequality (1), with \(p=2\), supplies the needed bound \(p_i<2^{e_0+1}\).

We also use equal-sum padding. For every positive \(d\), the triple
\[
 T_d=\{d,2d,3d\}
\]
has two ways to contribute the same sum \(3d\): either choose \(\{3d\}\), using one term, or choose \(\{d,2d\}\), using two terms. Consequently, from \(T\) pairwise disjoint such triples, one can choose any number of terms between \(T\) and \(2T\), always with the same total sum
\[
 W=3\sum d.                                               \tag{8}
\]
If all bases \(d\) are coprime to 6, distinct bases give disjoint triples: from an element of \(\{d,2d,3d\}\), one recovers \(d\) by first dividing by 2 if possible, otherwise by 3 if possible.

A divisor-pairing argument supplies enough small bases. For any positive \(R\), at least half its divisors are at most \(\sqrt R\), because a divisor larger than \(\sqrt R\) pairs injectively with the divisor \(R/d<\sqrt R\). Hence if
\[
 4T\le\tau(R),\qquad (4T)^2\le R,                        \tag{9}
\]
we can choose \(T\) divisors \(d\mid R\) with \(d^2\le R\) and \(4Td\le R\). If \((R,6)=1\), their triples are disjoint divisors of any multiple of \(6R\). Moreover (8) then satisfies the budget estimate used below, namely \(8W\le H\) when \(6R\mid H\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The reserve construction
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We now describe the central construction of a primitive representation at \(2H\). Assume \(323=17\cdot19\mid H\), and write \(H=323K\). In \(2H\) take
\[
 U=\{38K,34K\}.
\]
Both numbers divide \(646K=2H\), neither divides \(H\), and
\[
 \operatorname {lcm}(38K,34K)=646K=2H,
 \qquad \sum U=72K,
 \qquad 8\sum U\le2H.                                    \tag{10}
\]
Thus every set containing \(U\) already has lcm \(2H\).

Let \(A\) be a complete divisor set as in (7), with at most \(T\) elements. Choose a family \(F\) of \(T\) padding triples as above, with fixed padding sum \(W\). Finally choose a large reserve \(B\) of small divisors, disjoint from \(A,F,U\), whose total sum is small enough.

Select first exactly
\[
 n-|U|-2T=n-2-2T
\]
reserve elements. Let their sum be \(s_B\). We must fill the remaining sum
\[
 r=2H-s_B-W-\sum U.                                      \tag{11}
\]
The budget estimates ensure \(0\le r\le\sum A\), so completeness gives a subset \(C\subseteq A\) summing to \(r\). It uses at most \(T\) terms. Choose from the padding triples exactly \(2T-|C|\) terms; this lies between \(T\) and \(2T\), and their sum is \(W\). The union of the reserve choice, \(C\), this padding choice, and \(U\) therefore has exactly
\[
 (n-2-2T)+|C|+(2T-|C|)+2=n
\]
elements, and by (11) its sum is \(2H\). All are divisors of \(2H\), and (10) gives lcm \(2H\). This is a primitive \(n\)-representation.

For completeness, the small-divisor reserve itself follows from another divisor pairing. Put \(t=\tau(m)\), and let
\[
 G=\{d\mid m:2td\le m\}.
\]
A divisor excluded from \(G\) maps injectively under \(d\mapsto m/d\) into the divisors at most \(2t\). Thus, if
\[
 N+\#\{d\mid m:d\le2t\}\le t,                           \tag{12}
\]
then \(|G|\ge N\). Summing \(2td\le m\) over \(G\), and using \(|G|\le t\), gives
\[
 2\sum_{d\in G}d\le m.                                  \tag{13}
\]
Conditions (12) and (13), together with (7)--(10), give precisely the reserve and budget needed in (11).

Apply this with
\[
 R=\prod_{i=2}^{r-1}p_i^{e_i},
\]
so \((R,6)=1\), \(6R\mid H\), and
\[
 \tau(R)=\prod_{i=2}^{r-1}(e_i+1).
\]
For \(r\ge8\), \(17\cdot19\mid H\), as required.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Bounding the number of small divisors
--------------------------------------------------------------------

It remains to ensure (12). The only difficult term is the number of divisors of \(2H\) not exceeding \(2\tau(2H)\).

For \(d>0\), put \(w(d)=d^{-1/2}\), and
\[
 W(m)=\sum_{d\mid m}w(d).
\]
The divisor-product map shows
\[
 W(xy)\le W(x)W(y),                                      \tag{14}
\]
with equality when \(x,y\) are coprime. If \(c>1\) and
\[
 c^2\le(c-1)^2p,
\]
then the geometric sum over divisors of \(p^a\) is at most \(c\). For the first 25 primes use the rational values
\[
\frac1{1000}(3415,2367,1810,1608,1432,1384,1321,1298,1264,1229,
1219,1197,1186,1180,1171,1160,1150,1147,1140,1135,1133,1127,1124,1119,1114),
\]
and thereafter use \(10/9\). Direct squaring verifies the displayed inequality for each of the first 25 primes; for later primes it follows from \(p\ge101\). If \(P_r\) is the product of these factors, then
\[
 P_{25}\le1100,
 \qquad P_{25+t}\le1100(10/9)^t.                         \tag{15}
\]
Therefore \(W(2H)\le P_r\).

If \(q\) divisors of \(m\) are at most \(L\), each contributes at least \(L^{-1/2}\) to \(W(m)\), so
\[
 q\le\sqrt L\,W(m).

after squaring,
\[
 q\le K\quad\hbox{whenever}\quad LP_r^2\le K^2.         \tag{16}
\]
This is the inverse-square-root moment estimate.

For the uniform large case, write \(r=25+t\), and take
\[
 T=8r^3.
\]
Bertrand's estimate \(p_{i+1}\le2p_i\), beginning with \(p_{25}=101\), gives
\[
 p_{25+t}<2^{t+7}.
\]
Using (2) with the absent prime \(p_r\) gives
\[
 e_0+2\le16+2t.                                          \tag{17}
\]
Also every tail exponent is positive, whence
\[
 \prod_{i=k}^{r-1}(e_i+1)\ge2^{r-k}.                     \tag{18}
\]
The lower bounds in (3), evaluated at \(p_{24}=97\), sharpen (18) to
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^{r-1}(e_i+1)\ge45\,2^{r-4}=45\,2^{21+t}.    \tag{19}
\]
Indeed \(e_1\ge4,e_2\ge2,e_3\ge2\), contributing \(5\cdot3\cdot3=45\), and every later factor contributes at least 2.

The elementary induction
\[
 32(25+t)^3\le2^{23+t}                                   \tag{20}
\]
implies all the size conditions for the coin and padding construction:
\[
 4T+2\le\tau(H),\quad
 4T\le\tau(R),\quad
 (4T)^2\le R,
 \quad 2T\le\prod_{i=1}^{r-1}(e_i+1).                   \tag{21}
\]
Here \(R\ge4^{r-2}\), and (18)--(20) give the stated inequalities.

Finally, combining (15), (17), and (19), a direct induction on \(t\) gives
\[
2(16+2t)1100^2(100/81)^t
 \le \frac9{16}\,45\,2^{21+t}.                          \tag{22}
\]
Since \(8T\) is at most the right-hand tail count in (19), (22) implies
\[
 2\tau(2H)P_r^2
 \le\left(\prod_{i=1}^{r-1}(e_i+1)-2T\right)^2.          \tag{23}
\]
Putting \(L=2\tau(2H)\) in (16), (23) supplies (12), and hence the reserve construction. We have proved:

**Large case.** If an \(n\)-minimal integer \(H\) has at least 25 distinct prime factors, then \(2H\) has a primitive \(n\)-representation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The finite case of fewer than 25 prime factors
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We now describe the exhaustive finite calculation used for \(r<25\). This description includes both the enumeration and the tests, so that exhaustiveness does not depend on guessing a list of likely integers.

For fixed \(r<25\), enumerate every nonincreasing positive vector
\[
 (e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})

after imposing exactly the bounds (3):
\[
 \max\{1,\lfloor\log_{p_i}p_{r-1}\rfloor\}
 \le e_i\le2\lfloor\log_{p_i}p_r\rfloor.
\]
Recursively choose \(e_0,e_1,\ldots\), with each choice no larger than the preceding one. The structural results of Section 2 prove that the exponent vector of every minimal \(H\) occurs in this enumeration.

The enumerated vectors are compressed by divisor records. A vector \(e\), representing
\[
 N(e)=\prod_{i<r}p_i^{e_i},\qquad T(e)=\prod_{i<r}(e_i+1),
\]
is assigned a record \(f\) satisfying
\[
 N(f)\le N(e),\qquad T(f)\ge T(e).
\]
The resulting record table contains 796 vectors. Its first entries, for orientation, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
f&N(f)&T(f)\\ \hline
()&1&1\\
(1)&2&2\\
(2)&4&3\\
(1,1)&6&4\\
(2,1)&12&6\\
(3,1)&24&8\\
(2,2)&36&9\\
(4,1)&48&10\\
(2,1,1)&60&12\\
(3,1,1)&120&16
\end{array}
\]
and the table continues through all 796 undominated records. The two displayed inequalities are checked by integer products. If \(H=N(e)\) is \(n\)-minimal, then \(n\le T(e)\le T(f)\), so minimality gives \(H\le N(f)\). Together with \(N(f)\le H\), this forces \(H=N(f)\). Thus every minimal \(H\) with \(r<25\) is exactly one of the 796 record values.

Each record is then discharged by one of the following mathematically explicit certificates.

1. **Direct witnesses up to divisor count 512.** For each \(3\le n\le512\), except the nine values in \(E\), an increasing list of \(n\) divisors is supplied whose sum and lcm equal a stated integer \(w\). For each of the first 50 records, whose divisor counts run through the successive record values up to 512, these witnesses satisfy \(w\le2N(f)\). Minimality locates \(n\) between the divisor count of the preceding record and that of the present one, so the appropriate witness applies. The boundary record is
\[
 f=(7,3,1,1,1,1),\qquad T(f)=512.
\]
Every supplied list is checked simply by confirming that it is strictly increasing, every entry divides \(w\), its length is \(n\), its sum is \(w\), and its iterated lcm is \(w\).

2. **Moment certificates.** For records of length 8 through 24, the conditions in (21) are checked with \(T=C(H)\). The small-divisor estimate is strengthened, where useful, to a cubic moment. For positive \(k\), define
\[
 W_k(m)=\sum_{d\mid m}d^{-1/k}.
\]
Exactly as in (14)--(16), if \(W_k(m)\le B\), then the number of divisors at most \(L\) is at most \(K\) whenever \(LB^k\le K^k\). For \(k=3\), denominator \(100000\), the rational numerators used for the first 24 primes are
\[
79371,69337,58481,52276,44965,42530,38892,37476,35164,32549,
31834,30011,29001,28544,27710,26623,25688,25404,24622,24150,
23928,23306,22925,22398.
\]
For each \(i\), cubing verifies
\[
100000^3\le q_i^3p_i.
\]
Finite geometric sums then give an integer numerator and denominator for an upper bound on \(W_3(2H)\). The certificate checks the resulting cubic inequality and hence the required small-divisor count.

3. **Exact divisor-count certificates.** Divisors of
\(2H=2^{e_0+1}\prod_{i>0}p_i^{e_i}\) are generated recursively: from the divisor list for the remaining prime powers, append \(1,p,\ldots,p^e\) times every tail divisor. Filtering this list at a cutoff \(L\) gives exactly the number and sum of divisors at most \(L\). Thus the reserve inequality (12) can be checked directly by integer recursion, with no unexamined divisors.

4. **Explicit reserve certificates.** In the few cases where the generic choice is inefficient, the certificate supplies the complete coin list, the list of padding bases, the two lcm-forcing divisors, and a cutoff. Completeness of the coin list is checked successively by (5). Divisibility, disjointness, cardinalities, lcm, and budget are checked directly. The recursive bounded-divisor count and sum described in item 3 then prove that enough reserve divisors remain. Section 4 turns these data into the required primitive representation.

For records beyond the first 50, a certificate proves either \(n\le512\) or directly constructs a primitive representation at \(2H\). But these record values are strictly larger than
\[
 N(7,3,1,1,1,1),
\]
which already has 512 divisors. If \(n\le512\), minimality would force \(H\le N(7,3,1,1,1,1)\), a contradiction. Hence the primitive alternative always holds.

This exhaustive record calculation proves:

**Finite case.** If \(3\le n\), \(n\notin E\), and an \(n\)-minimal \(H\) has fewer than 25 prime factors, then some \(w\le2H\) has a primitive \(n\)-representation.

Together with the large case, this proves the twice-bound theorem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Direct exceptional calculations
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For the seven exceptional values other than 4 and 5, the following sets give primitive representations:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|l}
n&m&D\\ \hline
8&60&1,2,4,5,6,10,12,20\\
9&84&1,2,3,4,6,7,12,21,28\\
10&120&2,3,5,6,8,10,12,20,24,30\\
16&360&3,4,5,6,8,9,10,15,18,20,24,30,36,40,60,72\\
20&672&1,2,3,4,6,7,8,12,14,16,21,24,28,32,42,48,56,84,96,168\\
24&840&1,3,4,5,6,7,8,10,12,14,20,21,24,28,30,35,40,42,56,60,70,84,120,140\\
30&1680&2,4,5,6,7,8,10,14,15,16,20,21,24,28,30,35,40,42,48,56,60,70,80,84,105,112,120,168,210,240.
\end{array}
\]
In each row the entries are distinct divisors of \(m\), and direct addition and lcm calculation give both sum and lcm equal to \(m\).

A complete subset search shows that no smaller positive integer has even an ordinary representation for the corresponding \(n\). Here is the exhaustive search used, including its pruning rule. List the divisors of \(m\) in descending order. A recursive state consists of the unused suffix, the number \(c\) of terms still required, the remaining target sum \(s\), and, when needed, the lcm accumulated so far. Branch on excluding or including the first divisor. The include branch replaces \((c,s,g)\) by
\[
(c-1,s-d,\operatorname {lcm}(g,d)).
\]
A branch is discarded if \(c\) exceeds the number of unused divisors, or if \(s\) is smaller than the sum of the \(c\) smallest unused divisors, or larger than the sum of the \(c\) largest unused divisors. These are necessary bounds for every possible continuation. When \(c=0\), accept exactly when \(s=0\), and, for a primitive search, when the accumulated lcm is also \(m\). Induction on the divisor list proves that this recursion finds every possible subset: any solution either omits or contains the first divisor, and then lies in the corresponding recursive branch; the pruning inequalities cannot discard a solution.

Running this finite recursion gives no ordinary representation for
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
n&0\le m<M\\ \hline
8& M=60\\9&M=84\\10&M=120\\16&M=360\\20&M=672\\24&M=840\\30&M=1680.
\end{array}
\]
Therefore, if an ordinary representation occurs at any \(m\), the displayed primitive value \(M\) is at most \(m\). Thus domination also holds for these seven exceptional values.

For \(n=4\), there is an ordinary representation at 12,
\[
12=1+2+3+6,
\]
using four distinct divisors. A primitive representation exists at 18:
\[
18=1+2+6+9,
\qquad \operatorname {lcm}(1,2,6,9)=18.
\]
The same complete recursion finds no primitive four-term representation for any \(m\le12\). Hence
\[
 \mathrm{A081512}(4)\le12<a(4).
\]

For \(n=5\), there is an ordinary representation at 24,
\[
24=1+2+3+6+12.
\]
A primitive representation exists at 30:
\[
30=1+3+5+6+15,
\qquad \operatorname {lcm}(1,3,5,6,15)=30.
\]
The complete recursion finds no primitive five-term representation for any \(m\le24\). Consequently
\[
 \mathrm{A081512}(5)\le24<a(5).
\]
(The primitive witness at 30 is only an upper bound; no exact value of \(a(5)\) is needed for the strict inequality.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For every \(n\ne4,5\), the elementary arguments for \(n=0,1,2\), the twice-bound theorem for nonexceptional \(n\ge3\), and the seven direct exceptional calculations together show:

> every ordinary \(n\)-representation at \(m\) is dominated by a primitive \(n\)-representation at some \(w\le m\).

Taking minima gives
\[
 a(n)\le\mathrm{A081512}(n).
\]
On the other hand, every primitive representation is an ordinary one, so whenever either minimum is positive,
\[
 \mathrm{A081512}(n)\le a(n),
\]
and the empty cases agree as well. In particular strict inequality is impossible when \(n\ne4,5\).

For \(n=4\) and \(n=5\), the direct calculations above prove strict inequality. Therefore
\[
\boxed{\ a(n)>\mathrm{A081512}(n)\iff n=4\text{ or }n=5.\ }
\]
